Name: Karen Neff
Question: Would you consider the war between liberals and conservatives a war between the elites and the people?
Answer: What constitutes “elite" and “the people"? Both my parents, born in the 1920s, came form generational wealth, both monetarily and in real estate. Despite that head start, my parents were solidly middle class. Dad was an electrician, while mom was a SAHM. Because of my grandparents, I got 2 college degrees and a house in a quaint small town. I retired at 58 with a pension and health insurance. By some definition, I am an “elite", though I consider myself part of “the people". I am extremely liberal: pro-choice, LBGTQ+ ally, solid Democrat voter, for sane gun laws, etc … What does “liberal and “conservative“ mean to you? In bygone days, those terms were ways to interpret the Constitution. Liberal seeing the document as a living blueprint for governance. Open to reinterpretation based on changing science and information. Conservative interpretation meant the Constitution was written in stone, what was written was what was meant. Today, I don't think those definitions apply. Liberals want what benefits the most people, fair taxation of the wealthy, improved infrastructure, health care for all, respect for individual bodily autonomy, etc… Conservatives, in my humble opinion, want the opposite: kowtow to the ultra rich with outrageous tax credits, cutting benefits for the needy, inferior education delivered by unfunded public schools, keeping women at the mercy of biology and men… I know which side I'm on.

Question: Why do the average Americans retire at 62 years of age instead of 67? Isn’t it better to retire late to get the most out of social security?
Answer: My father died 13 months after retiring at 67. His final piece of advice to me was do not spend your life working. He wanted to travel, explore, and have fun, but a cancer diagnosis stopped all that cold. I retired after 31 years of teaching, at 58. I was sick of the administrative hoops, the paperwork, and the general bull $&%!. I've reconnected with long time friends and family, traveled, started an exercise routine, and enjoying life in general. I have not started collecting SS, and won't for another year. My husband, who retired at 70 and does get SS, and I live comfortably in our own home on his SS and my teachers pension. We have no credit debt, and 1 car payment. We're doing well. Life is short. Get out there and enjoy it.

Question: Back when women used to be housewives, is it true that they still worked, but only until they were married and/or had children? Was there ever a time women did not work AT ALL?
Answer: Women have always worked, whether in the home or out, usually both. In agrarian and hunter/gathering societies, women worked side by side with their partners: planting, working the fields, tending the animals, preparing meals, caring for the children, making fabrics for clothing. Their labor was necessary for the family to survive. In the industrial age women's labor was directed to more domestic areas: sewing, weaving, domestic maintenance (housekeeping for others), and in times of war, women were used to replace the men going into the military. As a footnote, house work is WORK!

Question: I bought sandals for my daughter. She said she doesn't like them and doesn't wear sandals. I buy her sandals every spring. She's mad that I went to the mall while she was out of town for the weekend with her dad. How would you handle this?
Answer: My mother did this constantly. Shoes, coats, bathing suits,… name it. Her excuse was I was difficult to shop with. Translation: you don't dress the way I want you to. The one time we shopped together, it was for my new bedroom. I wanted bold colors and geometric patterns. She wanted flowing flowers. I wanted a bold, royal blue. She demanded green. After weeks of arguing we went to the paint store to finally “pick out the damned color". I had extracted a promise that I could puck the shade of green. She was so relieved I was off the blue idea, she agreed immediately. I chose a color called DEEP JUNGLE GREEN. Think lime green on acid. She promised I could pick the shade. Karen won! You don't say how old she is but if she's wanting a voice in selecting her clothes, is it really that difficult to give her that? Perhaps give her a budget and shop WITH HER and not FOR HER.

Question: Do you believe that colleges are too liberal and attempt to indoctrinate or brainwash students, as suggested by 41 percent of those with little or no confidence in higher education? Why or why not?
Answer: I would hazard to say that the 41% with little or no confidence in higher education have barely finished high school. They have no idea what they're talking about. College will guide students to explore topics in their field of study, to think beyond the simple answers. It stands to reason that in doing so the students start asking bigger questions regarding the world around them and things they grew up believing to be truth. I grew up in a big republican family, attending rallies for state elected office, and believing what Nixon said and did was right, because he was the president. Then I started learning about Vietnam and the war. By the time I finished college, I was questioning everything I had grown up believing. Reagan pushed me over the edge, and I now am so firmly in the Democrat column, I can't imagine a Republican ever getting my vote.

Question: Has a parent ever had their child in one of their classes? How was the experience for both of them?

Can they divorce the role of parent from that of teacher? Do they expect more from their children than the average Joe or Jane walking into their classroom? Question: Is it common for parents to yell at their children due to stress rather than their behavior?
Answer: Of course stress plays a roll. Sadly, that doesn't ease the damage caused to the child. It teaches them that while they aren't allowed to have tantrums, yell, or lash out, it's perfectly acceptable for an adult to do the exact same thing. Additionally, to a child's mind, it makes the child responsible for the happiness of the adult. That's a huge burden for a child to carry into adulthood. In short, an adult needs to recognize their stressor and find constructive ways to release them. Yelling only spreads the stress to little ones who don't understand.

Question: Have you ever encountered a student teacher who was just terrible at teaching?
Answer: Ooh, pick me! I had Ben teaching 20+ years and never had a student teacher. I taught everything music, so it would have been a broad-based experience. Finally, a local college was sending out their first batch of music student teachers, and I got one. Her packet said she was in the Honors Program, top of her class, so I'm thinking I'm getting a gem. HA! When studying music, students generally have a instrument or vocal major, like flute, piano, or voice. I ask my S.T. what their major was. “Music" was the rocket scientist's answer. I'm thinking she misunderstood the question, so I ask was she a piano, voice, or instrumental major. Again “I studied music.” was the answer. I ask “what instrument do you play? “All of them" . Finally, WHAT WAS YOUR MAIN INSTRUMENT? I get this blank look and “well, I guess I'm pretty good at piano." Great! I stink at piano, so I give her an easy piano piece that any piano major should be able to sight read. I let her take the piece home to work it over, come back the next day and accompany the choir. She comes in, and the choir files in for first period. I lead them through warm up and introduce the ST. They get out the piece, which they have all but memorized, and off they go. Right away I realize something is very wrong. They finish the song, ST turns to me and says, loudly, that they don't seem to know the piece well. I tried to be diplomatic when I asked her what the key signature was. “Oh! It has 2 flats!” <students face palm> Her next assignment involved teaching 6th grade general music from a music magazine. There was a student reading section, teacher questions for discussion, vocabulary, and a listening section. One of the vocabulary words was INDIGENOUS. The teacher's guide has the definition in age appropriate terms, but the brainiac goes off of their own saying she's indigenous to this school. Now, these 6th graders were VERY bright. The ST goes on about being indigenous this or that, digging themselves into a massively deep hole. I step in because the kiddos look completely lost. “Kids, kangaroos are indigenous to Australia.” OH! NATIVE TO! 25 6th graders answer in perfect unison. Yeah, honors student, my ass. She talked about her personal life, watching a particular movie we were discussing, while in bed with her boyfriend. She covered the entire history of jazz without listening examples, (because she left all the ones I'd lent her at home and she had none listed to play from YouTube), used noted from her college class, never mentioned the Black/slavery relationship, New Orleans, or the Mississippi River once. And she did it ALL in one 45 minute class. She couldn't direct a 2 pattern to direct the band. Needless to say, I failed her. I later found that I was the second failed placement. The college allowed her to walk the stage for graduation, and go through 2 more placements to earn her teaching certificate.

Question: Can parents legally kick their child out the day they turn 18?
Answer: Your question is regarding the legality of kicking a child out of the house at 18, not the appropriateness. In the US, 18 is the age of majority, so yes, I've known parents who legally kicked their daughters out at their 18th birthday. One of them turned 18 on August 1st, just before the start of her senior year. She had nowhere to go, so she moved in with, you guessed it, the pedophile who'd been grooming her for years. She dropped out, and it took her 10 years to get her GED. Personally, I think kicking your child out before graduation, without any or limited means of support is cruel. I could get behind setting up a plan to lead them toward independence, or add responsibilities within the household, but that has been that child's home/refuge for 18 years, and to be summarily removed because of a birthday says volumes about what sort of person YOU are, and ain't none of it good.

Question: Should parents ask the opinion of their first child when deciding on having a second child?
Answer: I was 2 when my brother was born. What the heck did I know about anything. So at that point, asking would have been pointless. When I was 15 or 16 my mom came to me with a stupid grin on her face, asking if I'd like a little brother or sister. Having been made responsible at a very young age for a younger brother, and knowing my mom would fully look to me to “help" i.e. do the actual raising, I honestly and firmly said “NO". She looked surprised and a little disappointed. I had college plans that did not include sticking around to be a 3 parent to a child not my own. Never ask if you don't want to be told no.

Name: Karen Neff
Question: Is it appropriate for a guy to ask his female friend to live together on campus during college? Does this indicate romantic interest or is he simply looking for a roommate?
Answer: It wasn't on campus. In the 1970's that would have been a BIGno-no. It was during student teaching. Chris and I were doing our student teaching in the same town. He suggested that we find a furnished apartment in the town so we could save money on gas. I said yes, and the wheels started rolling. I asked my parents if I could live off campus with “a friend" named Chris. They agreed. I kept them abreast with all pertinent information, leaving out the fact that he was a he. Oh, and he was gay. The week before we were supposed to move in was Parents Weekend, and they wanted to meet Chris. I decided lunch at a local restaurant would be safest. I met my parents at 12, and told Chris at 12:15. “Mom, Dad, about Chris…he's a guy.” Total silence. Panicked glances passed between them. “…and he's gay.” Dad laughed, mom thanked God. Chris enters and they loved him. Loved him to the point that mom wanted me to “change" him. To be honest, he was pretty amazing, and probably the best roommate anyone could ask for.

Question: What are the potential consequences of teachers using sarcasm when talking or disciplining their students?
Answer: “Know your audience" should be your guide when using sarcasm. Most students don't understand the subtle art and are apt to take what you say literally. The only exception would be with students you know well, and who know and trust you. I had most of my students since 6th grade. We spoke the same language. I usually followed up my sarcastic comments with a massive eyeroll, or some other facial exaggeration, so they knew I was not serious.

Question: What was the worst math teacher you had in your high school?

The higher the grade, the closer you sat to the front of the room. Alphabetically, I would have been in the middle of the room, but grade-wise I was seated in the farthest reaches of the room. The result was my grade got even lower. She left after Christmas and Mr. Cannon took over. He was aptly named. He had a big, booming voice that demanded your attention. His seating plan also moved me closer to the front. And it didn't hurt that he was easy on the eye. My grades shot way up. The other was my algebra II teacher. He went over the skill, made the assignment then sat down and read the farm reports. I learned nothing, but somehow passed anyway.

Name: Karen Neff
Question: Do people who have been smoking for their entire lives typically stop when they become aware of the potential harm it can cause in the future?
Answer: My mom literally watch her father and Uncles die from cancers related to smoking. She knew the risks. Her mother pleaded with her. I pleaded with her. I hid her cigarettes. I used the economic argument, as she frequently complained about the rising costs and our lack of money. She knew all the harm smoking did, but she didn't care. “You have to die of something" was her favorite line. She went on O² at age 64, with congestive heart failure. She became a virtual prisoner of her home, dependent upon others for her well-being. She missed her grandchildren's school events, my wedding, visiting friends and family, everything. She died just after her 70th birthday, with total organ failure. But hey, you have to die of something, right?
